The Missing Piece in LLM Memory: Why Long Context and Retrieval Aren't Enough for Belief Revision

Community Article Published
October 15, 2026 Upvote 53 Rahul Vimalkanth boltwave Tanish Chudiwal tanish090905

Part I of Beyond Recall: The Mechanics of LLM Memory

A two-part series on how language models store, update, and revise information.

TL;DR: Why LLMs Struggle When Information Changes

A language model can retain a million tokens of context and still act on information that is no longer true. The problem isn't always forgetting. Sometimes, the information is still there, but the model fails to account for what has changed. This article explores the difference between keeping information accessible and revising what memory represents.

Access is not revision. Long context and retrieval help models retain and access past information. But when new evidence contradicts an earlier observation, having both available doesn't determine which one should govern the next answer. That depends on how memory is updated, read, or both.
Linear attention makes memory updates easier to examine. Standard softmax attention preserves an explicit history of keys and values, while linear attention compresses that history into a fixed-size recurrent state. Its simple update equations let us inspect what happens as new information accumulates, making it a useful starting point for understanding memory rather than a complete theory of it.
Accumulation works until something needs to change. Additive memory can store associations and combine repeated observations, which is useful when the underlying information remains consistent. But when a new fact replaces an old one, simply adding another association mixes the two instead of overwriting the outdated value. Overlapping keys introduce another problem: interference between stored associations.
Revision depends on what the write does. One way to correct an existing association is to compare what memory currently predicts with what the new observation says it should predict, then update using the difference. This is the idea behind the delta rule, and where Part II begins.

Architectures and memory systems discussed: softmax attention, KV caches, RAG, linear attention, Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), RetNet, Dragon Hatchling (BDH), Mamba, gated linear attention, xLSTM (mLSTM), DeltaNet, test-time training (TTT), and Titans.

Introduction

A model can read a million tokens and still fail to remember. That claim should feel slightly wrong. The tokens are there, the keys and values are there, and retrieval can surface information from far back in the sequence. What else could remembering require?
If you have spent a long research or coding session with a large language model, you may have seen the problem in practice. The relevant information is technically still available, yet the model starts relying on an assumption that was corrected much earlier, loses track of an intermediate decision, or behaves as though a later change had never happened. Modern models can hold very large contexts, but simply keeping information accessible does not guarantee that it will continue to be used correctly. This degradation is often described as context rot.
Longer contexts help with access to the past. They do not, by themselves, tell the model what should happen when the past becomes outdated. The system must also decide what the new observation should do to the state produced by the old one.

Retaining access to the past is not necessarily the same operation as revising it.

That distinction matters increasingly as language models become components of systems that act over time. A coding agent may work against a repository that changes during the session. A research agent may encounter evidence that weakens an earlier hypothesis. A robot may discover that a route that was open a few minutes ago is now blocked. A world model may have to decide whether an unusual observation is noise or evidence that the environment itself has changed.
Modern systems already have several ways to keep history nearby. Long context windows retain more tokens. Retrieval systems surface relevant records from external stores (Lewis et al., 2020; Khandelwal et al., 2020), though surfacing a record does not decide which one governs. Key–value caches preserve intermediate attention state during generation. External-memory variants such as Memorizing Transformers add a separate retrieval mechanism (Wu et al., 2022). Recurrent and state space models compress a growing history into bounded state. Fast-weight systems modify temporary parameters while a sequence is processed (Ba et al., 2016; Schlag et al., 2021). Each keeps history in a different form, so each handles conflicting evidence differently.
When new evidence arrives, does the system append it, compress it, average it with what is already stored, overwrite something, decay older state, or compute a targeted correction? That question gives us a way to compare systems that otherwise look quite different. We will call it update semantics.
Update semantics: what a new observation does to the state, and how that state is read afterward.
There is already a large literature on memory. This series is not an attempt to replace it with another taxonomy or to survey every attention architecture. Update semantics is a narrower lens, a framework for understanding memory updates.
Throughout this series, belief is meant operationally, not psychologically. It is what the system would return, and therefore how it would act, if queried right now. "Revising a belief" means changing that answer, whether by rewriting stored state or by changing how that state is read. We make this precise in Section 3.
This article uses linear attention as a concrete example because its associative memory state makes updates directly inspectable. By following what happens when observations accumulate, agree, or conflict, we can distinguish retaining information from revising an association. It assumes the reader has a basic understanding of self-attention, vectors, dot-products and matrix multiplication.
Part I develops that distinction from ordinary attention through associative memory. We will see where simple accumulation works remarkably well, where it begins to interfere with itself, and why the raw additive write alone does not implement replacement.
Part II begins with one correction mechanism for this memory: an update based on the difference between its current prediction and the new target.

1. What Is LLM Memory?

The word memory is used broadly in current language model research.
A context window is called memory. A retrieval database is called memory. Model parameters are often described as memory. So are recurrent state vectors, KV caches, fast weight matrices, and the parameters of small models adapted during inference.
We therefore need a definition broad enough to include these systems, but precise enough to reason about how they change.
Zhang et al. (2025) describe LLM memory as persistent state that can be written during pretraining, fine tuning, or inference, addressed later, and used to stably influence outputs.
For our purposes, it is useful to distinguish two broad kinds of memory.

Parametric memory is information represented in the model parameters. This includes much of the model's learned knowledge, feature representations, and reasoning priors.
Sequence memory, which we will also call mutable memory, is state that can change while the system processes a sequence or interacts with an environment. Depending on the architecture, this might be a context window and KV cache, a recurrent state vector, a fast weight matrix, the parameters of a small model adapted during inference, or plastic synaptic state.

This series is about the second kind.
The choice is deliberate. Suppose an agent learns that a function signature has changed. Retraining its base model is not the relevant operation. The system already received the evidence. What matters is how the state it is using right now should incorporate it.
The same issue appears in other settings. A research agent has to revise a working hypothesis. A world model has to distinguish repeated noisy measurements from an actual transition in the environment. A long running assistant has to know whether a new instruction supplements an old one or replaces it. An embodied agent has to maintain enough stability to ignore sensor noise while remaining plastic enough to react when the world genuinely changes.
The memory substrate may differ. The underlying problem is similar: mutable state has to remain useful while new evidence arrives.
That is the version of memory we will study here.

Figure 1. LLM memory during inference: fixed weights, evolving state. During inference, base-model weights remain fixed while sequence state changes. That state may be a context/KV cache, recurrent state, or temporary fast weights. The arrays are schematic, not measured weights; memory need not be matrix-shaped or fixed-size.

2. Why Long Context Isn't Enough: Context Rot and Belief Revision

The context window is one implementation of sequence memory, and its mechanics already explain some familiar failure modes.
Full self attention has quadratic computational cost in sequence length during the attention operation (Vaswani et al., 2017). During autoregressive generation with a KV cache, each new query still attends over an increasingly large collection of previous keys and values.
More context therefore gives the model access to more history, but it also gives the read process more information to distinguish between.
Position matters as well. Models do not use information uniformly across a long sequence. The lost in the middle results of Liu et al. (2024), for example, show that information placed in the middle of a long context can be used less reliably than information near the beginning or end.
These effects contribute to what practitioners often call context rot. Recent work uses the term for performance degradation as input context grows (Chroma Research, 2025). This is related to, but distinct from, resolving conflicting versions of a fact: longer context can make information less reliably usable, while revision concerns what the system does when evidence changes.
But retrieval difficulty is only one part of the problem.
Suppose there is no clutter at all. Imagine a single fact sitting cleanly in memory, easy to retrieve, with no distractors competing against it.
Now consider what happens when that fact stops being true.
Suppose you are working on a relatively large codebase and an agent has been asked to refactor a service. This is not a trivia question. The agent has to call a function correctly.
Early in the session it reads:
get_user(user_id: str) -> User
Later, a teammate's merge changes the function to:
get_user(org_id: str, user_id: str) -> User
The agent discovers the change because its old call raises a TypeError.
If the system retains the full session, both observations may remain available:

get_user(user_id: str) -> User
get_user(org_id: str, user_id: str) -> User

Nothing has necessarily been forgotten in the ordinary sense.
Both records are present.
Yet presence is not enough. The agent still has to determine which signature governs its next action.
One system may preserve both observations and let attention prefer the later one. Another may attach timestamps and let a retrieval system favor the newer record. Another may overwrite some internal association. Another may gradually decay older state. Another may update only after a controller decides that the newer observation is reliable.
All of these systems may have seen exactly the same sequence.
Their behavior can still differ because their update semantics differ.
Long context therefore addresses a different problem from revision. It gives the system access to history. It does not, by itself, specify the semantics of change.
The important question becomes: what should a new observation do to the state that is already there?
To answer that systematically, we need a common language for memory updates.

3. How Does LLM Memory Update? The Update and Read Rules

Suppose a system already has some mutable state and then receives a new observation. We want to describe the transition without committing immediately to one particular architecture.
Let the observations be
x1,x2,…
x_1, x_2, \ldots
x1​,x2​,…
and let MtM_tMt​ denote the memory state after processing observation xtx_txt​.
We can write the update in the general form
Mt=Uθ(Mt−1,xt).
M_t = U_\theta(M_{t-1}, x_t).
Mt​=Uθ​(Mt−1​,xt​).
Here, MtM_tMt​ is not meant to represent a literal memory location. It is an abstract state describing what the system currently retains.
The terms have a simple interpretation:

Mt−1M_{t-1}Mt−1​ is the state before the new observation
xtx_txt​ is the incoming observation or write signal
MtM_tMt​ is the resulting state
UθU_\thetaUθ​ is the rule that determines how the transition happens

Why Use a General Memory Update Equation?

There are many possible abstractions for memory, so the choice deserves some justification.
The purpose of
Mt=Uθ(Mt−1,xt)
M_t = U_\theta(M_{t-1}, x_t)
Mt​=Uθ​(Mt−1​,xt​)
is not to claim that all memory systems are equivalent. They are not. Their representations, training procedures, computational costs, and inductive biases can differ substantially.
The equation is useful because it isolates the part of the problem we care about: the effect of new evidence on existing state.
For a standard KV cache, UθU_\thetaUθ​ largely appends.
For additive fast weight memory, it adds an outer product.
For a recurrent state with decay, some existing state is attenuated before new information is incorporated.
For a delta rule, the update depends on what the memory currently predicts.
For some test time learning systems, the update is an optimization step on mutable parameters.
The architectures remain different. The equation simply gives us one coordinate system in which to compare their state transitions.

Memory Updates vs. Memory Reads: Where Does Revision Happen?

The update equation tells us how stored state changes. It does not yet tell us what answer the system will return.
Suppose a query qtq_tqt​ arrives when memory is in state MtM_tMt​.
We can describe the read operation separately:
yt=Rθ(Mt,qt).
y_t = R_\theta(M_t, q_t).
yt​=Rθ​(Mt​,qt​).
This equation asks a different question: given the current state and a query, what should the system produce?
Separating UθU_\thetaUθ​ from RθR_\thetaRθ​ matters because what looks like revision from the outside can happen in either place.
Return to the function signature example. One system might directly modify its internal state when it discovers the new definition. In that case, revision happens inside UθU_\thetaUθ​.
Another system might retain both versions in an append only history and let the reader compare recency, provenance, source reliability, or execution outcomes. In that case, the stored records remain unchanged. The answer changes because RθR_\thetaRθ​ interprets them differently.
The outward behavior may be identical while the mechanisms are not.
Changing your mind can therefore mean rewriting the notebook or rereading the same notebook differently.
The opposite failure is possible too. A memory may update internally and still produce the wrong answer if the read rule retrieves or interprets the wrong part of the state.
Throughout this series, belief refers to the behavior induced jointly by the mutable state MMM and the read rule RRR. In practical terms, it is what the system returns, and therefore how it would act, when queried.
A useful way to organize the design space is
memory behavior=state representation+update signal+update rule+read rule+representation geometry.
\begin{aligned}
\text{memory behavior} ={}& \text{state representation} + \text{update signal} + \text{update rule} \\
&+ \text{read rule} + \text{representation geometry}.
\end{aligned}
memory behavior=​state representation+update signal+update rule+read rule+representation geometry.​
This should be read as a lens rather than a theorem. Its purpose is to make several design decisions explicit.
State. Is memory a vector, matrix, sequence, database, set of statistics, or the parameters of a small model?
Update signal. Does the system receive a token representation, key value pair, target, gradient, confidence score, or controller output?
Write construction. Is the write determined only by the incoming observation, or does it depend on the state already stored?
Read. Does retrieval use a dot product, normalization, search, a nonlinear predictor, or another learned process?
Timescale. Does state change per token, per chunk, per episode, or across deployment?
Reset boundary. When is mutable state cleared while slower parameters remain fixed?
Selectivity. Can the system choose not to write an observation?
Forgetting. Does information decay, get overwritten, become invalid through metadata, or remain until explicit eviction?
Edit locality. If one association changes, do nearby queries change as well because their representations overlap?
These choices expose familiar tradeoffs.
A highly plastic memory can revise quickly but may overreact to noise. A stable memory can preserve useful information but remain stale. Compression can reduce storage cost while increasing interference. Forgetting can remove outdated state while also removing information that was still useful.
Once update and read are separated, many memory systems become easier to compare without pretending that their architectures are identical.

Figure 2. LLM memory revision during writing or retrieval. When a function signature changes, a system can overwrite the indexed record or retain a history and resolve which version governs at read time. Both designs can return the current definition; they differ in where revision happens.

I. A Map to Return To

The equation
Mt=Uθ(Mt−1,xt),
M_t = U_{\theta}(M_{t-1}, x_t),
Mt​=Uθ​(Mt−1​,xt​),
does not determine how memory should respond to new information. It only gives us a common language for comparing update mechanisms. Across this two-part series, we return to the same question:

What should the update rule UθU_{\theta}Uθ​ do when a new observation conflicts with what the system already remembers?

The main answers considered in this series are:

Store more: Softmax KV caches and retrieval systems preserve explicit records of the past. They postpone revision to the read process, metadata, or an eventual eviction policy.
Compress: Linear attention, RetNet, and selective state-space models such as Mamba fold a growing history into a bounded recurrent state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023; Gu and Dao, 2023). They trade explicit historical detail for fixed memory and constant-cost updates.
Correct while writing: Delta rules read the memory’s current prediction and write the residual between that prediction and the new target. Gated linear attention and xLSTM variants use data-dependent gates or memory updates to control what is retained and incorporated; these mechanisms do not all explicitly consult the current prediction. Both are revision mechanisms, but only the delta family closes the loop through prediction error.
Learn at inference: Test-time training treats the mutable state as the parameters (or parameters and optimizer state) of a small model that is updated online as new evidence arrives.
Distribute plasticity: Synaptic and multi-store systems distribute working memory across edges, slots, or coupled state variables rather than placing it in one explicit memory matrix. Dragon Hatchling (BDH) is a recent example of this approach (Kosowski et al., 2025).

These mechanisms share the same abstract vocabulary, but they implement fundamentally different answers to the update question.

These approaches differ in what they do with the old state. While they are not mutually exclusive and some architectures employ more than one of these approaches, it is a useful notion to keep in mind. The rest of this series asks what each choice can and cannot do when the world changes.

III. Failure modes of the memory

Their failure modes therefore differ: stored history can become stale, compressed states can suffer interference, aggressive correction can overreact to noise, and selective forgetting can erase information prematurely.

Figure 3. Four failure modes of mutable LLM memory. An update may be too weak to revise a stale belief, insufficiently local and disturb unrelated associations, too strong and overshoot the new evidence, or paired with forgetting that removes useful information too soon. The panels illustrate distinct failure mechanisms rather than measured model behavior.
The sections that follow walk one associative-memory example end to end: what each architecture stores, how it writes, how it reads, and what happens when observations conflict.

4. Linear Attention as Associative Memory: From Softmax to Fast Weights

Attention is already associative.
Keys identify directions in representation space. Values carry information associated with those directions. Queries determine which stored values contribute to the output.
Standard softmax attention retains an explicit key value history.
Linear attention can instead compress that growing history into a fixed size recurrent state.

Figure 4. Softmax self-attention history versus a linear-attention recurrent state. Softmax self-attention reads from stored keys and values; linear attention compresses their contributions into a recurrent state. Feature maps and normalization are implicit in this schematic; the equations below specify the complete normalized read. Source: Understanding Linear Attention.
That change is usually discussed as a computational optimization. Here, we care about a second consequence: it changes the form of the memory itself.

Why Use Linear Attention to Study Memory?

There are many memory mechanisms we could start from.
Linear attention is useful here because its recurrent state is unusually transparent. In the fast weight view, memory becomes a matrix that can be written and read directly. We can see exactly what each observation contributes, what a query retrieves, when repeated writes help, and where interference enters.
That makes it a useful analytic baseline.
It is not being presented as a complete theory of memory.
We will move through three forms.
First, ordinary softmax attention keeps explicit history.
Second, normalized linear attention replaces that growing list with running statistics.
Third, an unnormalized fast weight form reduces the state to one associative matrix that is simple enough to inspect directly.
The point of the derivation is not merely to arrive at a more efficient attention equation. It is to expose the semantics of the write.

I. Softmax Attention: Explicit Associative Retrieval

A useful way to think about softmax attention is as an address book that keeps every entry it has seen. At step iii, the model stores a key kik_iki​, which acts like an address, together with a value viv_ivi​, which contains the associated information. When a query arrives, attention does not retrieve a single page directly. Instead, it compares the query with all stored keys and forms a weighted combination of their values.
Start from scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al., 2017):
Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax ⁣(QK⊤dk)V.
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.
Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V.
Here Q,K∈RL×dkQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_k}Q,K∈RL×dk​ and V∈RL×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_v}V∈RL×dv​. For the ttt-th query under a causal mask, restricted to positions i≤ti\le ti≤t, that expands to
yt=∑i=1tαti vi,αti=exp⁡ ⁣(qt⊤ki/dk)∑j=1texp⁡ ⁣(qt⊤kj/dk).
y_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{ti}\,v_i,\qquad
\alpha_{ti}=\frac{\exp\!\big(q_t^{\top}k_i/\sqrt{d_k}\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\exp\!\big(q_t^{\top}k_j/\sqrt{d_k}\big)}.
yt​=i=1∑t​αti​vi​,αti​=∑j=1t​exp(qt⊤​kj​/dk​​)exp(qt⊤​ki​/dk​​)​.
Here qt,ki∈Rdkq_t,k_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k}qt​,ki​∈Rdk​ and vi∈Rdvv_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}vi​∈Rdv​.
The interpretation is straightforward. The similarity qt⊤kiq_t^\top k_iqt⊤​ki​ determines how strongly the query matches a stored key, and the softmax converts those similarities into normalized weights. The output is therefore a similarity weighted mixture of the values associated with earlier keys.
At the KV-state level, memory is the raw list {(ki,vi)}\{(k_i,v_i)\}{(ki​,vi​)}, sized Θ ⁣(t(dk+dv))\Theta\!\big(t(d_k+d_v)\big)Θ(t(dk​+dv​))
During autoregressive decoding, every new token contributes another key value pair. The next query must attend over an increasingly large set of stored entries, so the work associated with reading the cache grows with sequence length.
The address book analogy is useful here for another reason. Writing a new entry does not edit an old page. If two observations describe different versions of the same underlying fact, both can remain in the cache. The model may learn to give the newer entry more weight when it reads the cache, but that is a property of the read process. The earlier key value pair has not been physically replaced.
So softmax attention gives us an explicit, append oriented associative memory. It preserves individual records well, but its state grows with the sequence and revision is left largely to the reader.
The natural next question is whether we can keep this associative form of retrieval without keeping the entire address book open. Linear attention does this by replacing the growing list of entries with a fixed size set of running statistics.

II. How Linear Attention Compresses the KV History

Katharopoulos et al. (2020) swap the softmax kernel for a feature map ϕ\phiϕ. For the normalized form, similarities must be non-negative and their total must be positive for the read to be a convex combination:
sim(q,k)=ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k).
\mathrm{sim}(q,k)=\phi(q)^{\top}\phi(k).
sim(q,k)=ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k).
Causal linearized attention then reads:
yt=∑i=1t[ϕ(qt)⊤ϕ(ki)]vi∑i=1tϕ(qt)⊤ϕ(ki)=St⊤ϕ(qt)zt⊤ϕ(qt).
\begin{aligned}
y_t
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t}
\bigl[\phi(q_t)^\top\phi(k_i)\bigr]v_i}
{\sum_{i=1}^{t}\phi(q_t)^\top\phi(k_i)} \\
&= \frac{S_t^\top\phi(q_t)}{z_t^\top\phi(q_t)}.
\end{aligned}
yt​​=∑i=1t​ϕ(qt​)⊤ϕ(ki​)∑i=1t​[ϕ(qt​)⊤ϕ(ki​)]vi​​=zt⊤​ϕ(qt​)St⊤​ϕ(qt​)​.​
The rewrite exposes the point: the numerator is a running matrix and the denominator is a running vector, so you need a fixed-size matrix and vector instead of the full list. The sums are order-independent, but that describes the accumulator only, not the whole model: the keys and values being summed still come from projections that can depend on position and earlier layers. Define the running store and its normalizer:
St=∑i=1tϕ(ki)vi⊤∈Rm×dv,zt=∑i=1tϕ(ki)∈Rm.
S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\phi(k_i)v_i^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_v},\qquad
z_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\phi(k_i)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.
St​=i=1∑t​ϕ(ki​)vi⊤​∈Rm×dv​,zt​=i=1∑t​ϕ(ki​)∈Rm.
Readout is
yt=St⊤ϕ(qt)zt⊤ϕ(qt).
y_t=\frac{S_t^{\top}\phi(q_t)}{z_t^{\top}\phi(q_t)}.
yt​=zt⊤​ϕ(qt​)St⊤​ϕ(qt​)​.
This assumes a positive denominator; implementations commonly include a safeguard for small denominators.
And both pieces update recursively:
St=St−1+ϕ(kt)vt⊤,zt=zt−1+ϕ(kt),S0=0,  z0=0.
S_t=S_{t-1}+\phi(k_t)v_t^{\top},\qquad
z_t=z_{t-1}+\phi(k_t),
\qquad S_0=0,\; z_0=0.
St​=St−1​+ϕ(kt​)vt⊤​,zt​=zt−1​+ϕ(kt​),S0​=0,z0​=0.
State size is Θ(m dv+m)\Theta(m\,d_v+m)Θ(mdv​+m). It no longer grows with ttt.
Let the feature map be ϕ:Rdk→Rm\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}ϕ:Rdk​→Rm. It changes the similarity kernel and lets an expanding sum collapse into fixed-size running totals, updated online. For fixed feature and value dimensions, the cost of the recurrent update and read no longer grows with the number of previously processed tokens.

III. Dropping the Normalizer Gives a Fast-Weight Notebook

The normalized formulation gives us a useful interpretation in terms of query-dependent weights, but it also requires a second running quantity. Dropping the normalizer gives up that interpretation in exchange for a simpler associative state: a single matrix that can be written and read directly. This makes the fast-weight formulation clearer and gives us the simple object used in the analysis that follows.
Unnormalized linear attention drops the softmax, and the denominator along with it, entirely. One more simplifying step turns this into something even more transparent: throw away ztz_tzt​ and take ϕ\phiϕ as the identity. With ϕ=id\phi=\mathrm{id}ϕ=id:
yt=∑i=1t(qt⊤ki) vi=Wtqt,Wt=∑i=1tvi⊗ki.
y_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}(q_t^{\top}k_i)\,v_i=W_t q_t,\qquad
W_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_i\otimes k_i.
yt​=i=1∑t​(qt⊤​ki​)vi​=Wt​qt​,Wt​=i=1∑t​vi​⊗ki​.
The two running totals collapse into a single matrix Wt=∑ivi⊗kiW_t=\sum_i v_i\otimes k_iWt​=∑i​vi​⊗ki​, and a query becomes nothing more than WtqtW_t q_tWt​qt​. This simplification is not without cost. Without normalization, the read is no longer a weighted average of the stored values, so its magnitude is not automatically bounded as the notebook accumulates bindings. 5. Why Additive Memory Struggles with Belief Revision

The analysis below isolates a raw additive update with supplied key–value pairs and a linear read. This is a limitation of that update rule, not an impossibility result for a complete model: an upstream network, controller, or read mechanism may supply state-dependent behavior.
The useful distinction, then, is not whether accumulation is good or bad.

The question is whether the stream asks the memory to accumulate, average, or replace.

Additive memory looks attractive on first contact for three separate reasons at once: under orthogonal keys it gives exact retrieval, under compatible noise it supports principled averaging, and under linear attention it gives a fixed-size recurrent state whose storage does not grow with sequence length.

I. The Additive Write

The simplest form of associative memory adds each new key–value pair to a fixed-size state. The raw rule has no explicit erase operation, although signed writes can cancel earlier contributions. The write and read equations make this behavior precise and provide a simple setting for analyzing retrieval and the interference that can arise between stored associations.

V. Why a Raw Additive Write Does Not Overwrite an Association

The raw additive outer-product rule has no explicit delete operation. Under the orthogonal-key assumption, removing an association for key kkk would require a write that cancels the stored contribution, something like −vk⊤-v k^\top−vk⊤, or else a separate validity bit consulted at read time. Overwriting is likewise not native: it requires writing the residual (vnew−vold)k⊤(v_{\mathrm{new}}-v_{\mathrm{old}})k^\top(vnew​−vold​)k⊤, which already assumes knowledge of voldv_{\mathrm{old}}vold​ from somewhere. Without a state-dependent updater, both deletion and overwrite have to be supplied by an external controller, or inferred by the read rule interpreting an append-only log.
The raw additive write can accumulate and, with a separate normalizer, support averaging. It does not itself consult the current read MkMkMk to construct a state-dependent correction. Without reading MkMkMk, or receiving an external residual, it has no correction path in the write itself. Long context preserves history; whether belief is revised depends on the read rule, which retention alone does not specify.
That residual points directly to the delta rule.

From Accumulation to Correction: What Part I Established

We began by separating two problems that are often discussed together: retaining access to the past and deciding how the past should change when new evidence arrives.
Long context mainly helps with the first problem. Revision concerns the second.
Separating the update rule from the read rule then gave us a way to locate where revision happens. A system can modify its stored state directly, or it can preserve conflicting records and resolve them later during retrieval.
Linear attention provided a useful analytic memory because its recurrent state can be written explicitly. In that representation, additive memory has real strengths. It can store associations, retrieve them exactly under an ideal geometry, and support principled averaging when repeated observations measure one stable latent quantity.
The same update behaves differently when the stream means replacement.
If a new observation makes an earlier value obsolete, summing or averaging the two does not implement the intended semantics. The raw additive write does not implement replacement. For the associative memory studied here, one way to obtain replacement is to write the difference between the new target and the current prediction. Other designs can overwrite an addressed slot or resolve conflicting records at read time.
Representation geometry adds another constraint. Shared state does not imply independent slots. When keys overlap, associations interfere, and a later edit may affect more than one query.
